pr_body:
Fixes #6302

a new command. a TUI for browsing gh extensions. uses `tview`.

I've tested this pretty extensively on mac, WSL, and Windows (windows terminal + powershell), but more QA is very welcome given the sensitivity of a UI like this in different terminal environments.

there is a [video demo](https://youtu.be/TNjp0ohI7UU)

## discussion points

- The code is not quite as organized as I would like but I've been working on this too long and just need to call it.
- the ReadmeGetter thing is mostly vestigial and could probably be inlined but I ran out of steam
- The test coverage is pretty good but not 100%. It felt like diminishing returns, but it's possible to further inject the dependencies around `tview.Application`

followed by #6540
pr_comments:
- [x] use IsStdoutTTY not CanPrompt
- [x] filter out anything that doesn't start with 'gh-'

I took this for a spin a bit today and overall functionality worked well. My biggest concern is the colors. This is what it looks like in my normal terminal. It was very difficult to read and use. This is what is looks like in the default terminal app. Much better. Clearly the issue is that my color scheme in my normal terminal has modified colors causing these difficulties. I think this is a common case where color schemes override colors and thus we cant control the experience for all our users. This made me think that we could put in some effort into making the display of the command agnostic of the terminal theme. Right now we specify colors using `tcell`, for example `tcell.ColorWhite`, which will use the terminals definition of that color (only for the base 16 terminal colors), but `tcell` also allows specifying colors by hex value, `tcell.Color(0xFFFFFF)` which will then not rely on the terminal color scheme. What are your thoughts on making our own hex code definitions for the colors we use so that they are consistently displayed?

@mislav

> 1. The gh ext browse command on first run seems to be stuck for about ~20 seconds, but in fact it is preloading data. This is because the spinner isn't visible; see line comments for more notes on this.

I've fixed this. I had to redirect stderr (turns out I didn't need to redirect out also) because the extension manager prints `git` output to stderr during an install. I just do that redirection after the spinner is done, now.

> 2. The lines of the README preview seem double-spaced, which looks wrong (see screenshot). My terminal width is 158.

I'm genuinely unsure how to affect this from looking at glamour's docs

> 3. README preview has broken-looking line wrapping (see screenshot).

Fixed by matching glamour's word wrap with the width of the readme textview.

> 4. README preview can be scrolled up/down with Page Up/Page Down, but I'm not sure if laptop users know how to find that on a keyboard that seemingly doesn't have those keys. On a MacBook Pro, the trick is to press Fn + Up/Down arrows.

I had assumed this was widespread knowledge for mac users (I use fn + up/down arrow all the time) but I might be wrong. I've called it out in the usage, but do you think we should explore another hotkey?

> 5. The spacing in the left sidebar that lists repos and their descriptions looks weird when some repos have descriptions but others not (see screenshot).

I've changed the code to print "no description provided" when description is blank. Not ideal, but will at least make things more visually consistent.

> 6. I think the Filter bar need not be visible until someone has entered filtering mode or when there is an active filter. Due to its prominent position, it might be distracting otherwise.

I waffled on this but feel that having it always visible is a hint that you _can_ filter. I'm worried about people not noticing the legend at the bottom and a tantalizing filter bar gives them a reason to look for it. More technically, I was not able to find an easy way to hide and show things with tview which was surprising so at this point I'm not inclined to hack at that (but would like to figure out good ways to do that in the future).

@samcoe I'm punting on color because I agree with @mislav about the relative safety of sticking with the primary colors as known to ANSI. I have tweaked it to not use purple, however, which I saw as the worst part of your color scheme and generally a color I could see being wildly different across people's terminals. I've switched instead to just using black and white for list titles and selected highlights.
This is ready for further review @mislav @samcoe

### Key > > 7\. README preview can be scrolled up/down with Page Up/Page Down, but I'm not sure if laptop users know how to find that on a keyboard that seemingly doesn't have those keys. On a MacBook Pro, the trick is to press Fn + Up/Down arrows. > > I had assumed this was widespread knowledge for mac users (I use fn + up/down arrow all the time) but I might be wrong. I've called it out in the usage, but do you think we should explore another hotkey? I learned about `Fn + Up/Down` through this discussion. 😅 In [fzf (Add shift-up and shift-down)](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/commit/417bca03dfa9a15a37d64678b5a4a175db6eb0a1) the default for `Up/Down` of the preview is `Shift+↑↓`. --- ### Milky I get a milky display on macOS 10.15 with the default terminal (bottom-left:`iTerm2`, top-right: `Terminal`). https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/92653266/200499381-c0242b4d-835f-4be4-a8b7-8749e70e232a.mp4 --- ### nit-pick - description for the bottom text These are just visual preferences for a different layout, which I think is more visually appealing (can be safely ignored by the author of this PR). #### Repo: [samtay/so](https://github.com/samtay/so) #### Repo: [dlvhdr/gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) --- PS: 🥇 A good addition to the cli tool.

@LangLangBart thanks for the feedback!

re: milkiness, it's unfortunate but I think we're stuck with it for now. I actually struggled to make tview set a background color application wide.

re: the help dialog, I do prefer the idea of having toggle-able help. It was an initial goal that I didn't get to.

I've opened up #6584 to capture this stuff (it already has toggle-able help) and some other followup work we'd like to do.

issue_context.title: gh ext browse
issue_context.body:
This issue covers a new command for `gh extension`. We've been calling it `gh ext manage` but I am starting to feel that `gh ext browse` is a better name, though with the caveat that it's totally different from `gh browse`. `gh ext explore` is also on the table.

This new command is a new thing for us; a rich TUI that takes over a terminal and is designed for human interaction exclusively.

The capabilities:

- list all gh extensions
- filter the list with a fuzzy search
- sort the list in different ways
- render the selected extension's readme in a sidepane
- have hotkeys for installing/uninstalling extensions

Design considerations:

- Highlight extensions that are 1st party (ie, in the `cli` repo)
- Cycle through sorting with options:
  - Installed
  - First party
  - Stars
  - Name
- Test with a screen reader; we assume that it will not be a pleasant consideration, so it's likely we'll cover this accessibility gap with an accompanying `gh extension search` command that is both scriptable and screen reader friendly (issue TBD).

To start I'll be spiking with bubbletea since the bubbles collection has the exact primitives we need for this. If it's not comfortable, we'll try a spike with tview.

review_comments: Maybe this could use an addition of `defer StopProgressIndicator()` so that the progress indicator is made to stop spinning in case of an error
What do you think about allowing the down key to also do `extList.Focus()`? I naturally reached for that key after I was done typing in my search filter.
